concepts.def: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. Each is a strong electrostatic attraction, but they differ in which particles are involved and in what happens to the outer electrons.
Bonding in which the particles are oppositely charged ions. It occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals, for example sodium chloride and magnesium oxide.

Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. It occurs in most non-metallic elements, such as oxygen and chlorine, and in compounds of non-metals, such as water and methane.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. It occurs in metallic elements and in alloys.

The force of attraction between opposite electric charges. All three types of strong bond are explained by electrostatic attraction: between oppositely charged ions in ionic bonding, between the shared pair of electrons and the two nuclei in covalent bonding, and between the metal atoms and the delocalised electrons they share in metallic bonding.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons. The charge arises because the number of electrons no longer equals the number of protons.
When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom, the electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred away. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions.
Non-metal atoms gain the electrons transferred from the metal atoms and so become negatively charged ions.

The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0). For example Na (2,8,1) forms Na+ with the structure 2,8, and Cl (2,8,7) forms Cl- with the structure 2,8,8.

A diagram that represents the electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound, using dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the electrons of the other so the transfer can be followed. Each ion is drawn in square brackets with its charge written outside.

The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number: Group 1 forms 1+ ions, Group 2 forms 2+ ions, Group 6 forms 2- ions and Group 7 forms 1- ions.

An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. There is no fixed small unit and no molecule - the regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions, called a lattice, continues throughout the whole substance.
Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice, and this is called ionic bonding.

The structure of sodium chloride can be represented as a dot and cross diagram, as a ball and stick model, and as two-dimensional and three-dimensional diagrams of the lattice. A diagram showing a regular repeating arrangement of oppositely charged particles tells you the compound is ionic.

concepts.term: Empirical formula of an ionic compound
concepts.def: The simplest whole number ratio of the ions in the structure. It is worked out from a given model or diagram by counting the ions of each type and reducing the count to its simplest ratio - so a model with 4 sodium ions and 4 chloride ions gives NaCl, not Na4Cl4.

concepts.term: Limitations of models of a giant ionic structure
concepts.def: A dot and cross diagram shows where the electrons have come from but shows nothing about how the ions are arranged. A ball and stick model shows the arrangement but the sticks are not real and the ions are drawn much too far apart. A two-dimensional diagram cannot show that the lattice extends in three dimensions, and every diagram shows only a tiny part of a structure that is in reality enormous.

When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. These bonds between atoms are strong. A single covalent bond is one shared pair; a double bond is two shared pairs and a triple bond is three.

A covalently bonded substance may consist of small molecules - a fixed, small number of atoms held together by covalent bonds, such as H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2. Common small molecules can be recognised from their chemical formula.
Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers. A polymer molecule is still a molecule - a very long chain built from a repeating unit - not a giant lattice.

Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide. Every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, so there are no separate molecules.

A diagram showing the outer electrons of the bonded atoms, with each shared pair drawn in the overlap between two atoms. Students should be able to draw these for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane - for example O2 has two shared pairs between the atoms and N2 has three.

A polymer is represented by drawing its repeating unit inside brackets with the subscript n outside, where n is a large number. The n does not stand for a particular value - it shows that the unit inside the brackets is repeated a great many times along the chain.

The covalent bonds in small molecules, in the repeating units of polymers and in part of giant covalent structures can be represented using a line to represent a single bond. One line stands for one shared pair of electrons, so a double bond is drawn as two lines.

concepts.term: Limitations of models of molecules and giant structures
concepts.def: A dot and cross diagram shows which atom each electron came from but not the shape of the molecule or the relative sizes of the atoms. A ball and stick model shows shape but exaggerates the space between atoms and shows bonds as solid sticks. Two-dimensional diagrams flatten a three-dimensional shape, and any diagram of a giant covalent structure can show only a small part of it.

The molecular formula is deduced from a model or diagram by counting the actual number of atoms of each element in the molecule, not the bonds between them, and not reducing the count to its simplest ratio. A model of ethane with 2 carbon and 6 hydrogen atoms is C2H6, not CH3.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern. The pattern continues throughout the whole piece of metal, so a metal has no molecules.

The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure. They no longer belong to any one atom. The sharing of these delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Metallic bonding occurs in alloys as well as in metallic elements, so brass and steel are held together by metallic bonds.

mcqs.q: In metallic bonding, the specification describes the particles as:
options: atoms that share delocalised electrons
positive ions attracted to negative ions
atoms that each keep their own outer electrons
atoms that share a single pair of electrons
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's wording: for metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.

mcqs.q: Magnesium oxide is formed from magnesium and oxygen. What bonding does it contain?
options: Ionic, because a metal has combined with a non-metal
Covalent, because two different elements have combined
Metallic, because one of the elements is a metal
Covalent, because oxygen needs two more electrons
mcqs.explain: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen a non-metal, and ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.

mcqs.q: Which statement about covalent bonding is correct?
options: It occurs only in compounds, and never in elements such as oxygen
It occurs whenever two atoms of different elements join together
It occurs in non-metal elements but not in compounds of non-metals
It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement for where covalent bonding is found.

mcqs.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. The bonding in brass is:
options: ionic, because copper and zinc are different elements
covalent, because the two metals share outer electrons
metallic in the copper but absent in the zinc
metallic, because metallic bonding occurs in alloys
mcqs.explain: The specification states that metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.

mcqs.q: Why is the ionic bond in sodium chloride described as strong?
options: There are strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
The transfer of the electron from sodium to chlorine is itself the bond
Pairs of electrons are shared strongly by the sodium and the chlorine
The ions are packed so tightly that they cannot physically move apart
mcqs.explain: Chemical bonding is explained in terms of electrostatic forces, and the ionic bond is the attraction between the ions formed.

mcqs.q: A sodium atom (2,8,1) reacts with a chlorine atom (2,8,7). What happens to the electrons?
options: Sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one electron
Sodium gains seven electrons to complete its outer shell
Sodium gains one electron and so becomes positively charged
Sodium and chlorine share one pair of electrons between them
mcqs.explain: Electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred; the metal loses and the non-metal gains.

mcqs.q: An oxygen atom has the electronic structure 2,6. What is the electronic structure of the oxide ion?
mcqs.explain: Oxygen is in Group 6, so it gains two electrons; 2,6 becomes 2,8, the electronic structure of neon.

mcqs.q: An element in Group 2 of the periodic table forms an ion. What is the charge on that ion?
mcqs.explain: Group 2 metals lose their two outer electrons, so the charge is 2+ and matches the group number.

mcqs.q: Potassium is in Group 1 and sulfur is in Group 6. Which pair of ion charges is correct?
options: K+ and S6-
K+ and S2-
K- and S2+
K2+ and S2-
mcqs.explain: Group 1 metals lose one electron to form 1+ ions; Group 6 non-metals gain two to form 2- ions.

mcqs.q: In a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride, the sodium ion should be drawn showing:
options: an empty outer shell, in square brackets with a + charge
one outer electron, in square brackets with a + charge
one outer electron, with no brackets and no charge shown
eight outer electrons, in square brackets with a - charge
mcqs.explain: After transfer sodium has 2,8, so no outer electrons are drawn, and the ion is shown in brackets with its charge.

mcqs.q: A dot and cross diagram is drawn for magnesium chloride. What should it show?
options: One chloride ion, with a charge of 2-
Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 7-
One chloride ion, with a charge of 1-
Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 1-
mcqs.explain: Magnesium loses two electrons, one to each chlorine atom, giving Mg2+ and two Cl- ions.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the bonding in a giant ionic lattice?
options: Each positive ion is bonded to one negative ion beside it
Electrons transfer continuously between the ions in the lattice
Strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between the ions
Weak forces act between ions that are themselves very strong
mcqs.explain: The specification states that these forces act in all directions in the lattice, and this is called ionic bonding.

mcqs.q: A diagram shows a regular repeating array of alternating Na+ and Cl- particles. What can be deduced?
options: It is molecular, because each sodium is paired with one chlorine
It is covalent, because sodium and chlorine share electrons here
It is metallic, because the particles form a regular pattern
It is ionic, because oppositely charged ions are arranged in a lattice
mcqs.explain: Charged particles arranged in a repeating lattice is the diagnostic feature of an ionic compound.

mcqs.q: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional diagram of the sodium chloride lattice?
options: It shows the ions touching when they are really far apart
It shows the wrong ratio of sodium ions to chloride ions
It shows ions rather than the molecules that are present
It cannot show that the lattice extends in three dimensions
mcqs.explain: A flat diagram loses the third dimension, so the forces acting in all directions cannot be shown.

mcqs.q: What is a limitation of using a ball and stick model for a giant structure?
options: It shows the particles at correct spacing but only in two dimensions
It cannot show the ratio in which the particles are joined
It shows the particles too far apart and bonds as solid sticks
It shows a giant structure as though it were one small molecule
mcqs.explain: Bonds are forces, not rods, and the model exaggerates the space between the particles.

mcqs.q: A model of an ionic compound shows 4 calcium ions and 8 fluoride ions. Its empirical formula is:
options: Ca4F8
CaF2
Ca2F
CaF
mcqs.explain: The ratio 4:8 simplifies to 1:2, and the empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio of the ions.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the covalent bonds inside a water molecule is correct?
options: They are weak, because water boils at quite a low temperature
They are formed by electrons transferring between the atoms
They are strong bonds between the atoms in the molecule
They are strong only where two pairs of electrons are shared
mcqs.explain: The specification states directly that the covalent bonds between atoms are strong.

mcqs.q: Which formula represents a substance that consists of small molecules?
options: NaCl
CO2
SiO2
Cu
mcqs.explain: Carbon and oxygen are both non-metals and carbon dioxide consists of small molecules.

mcqs.q: Poly(ethene) and diamond are both covalently bonded. Which statement is correct?
options: Poly(ethene) has very large molecules; diamond is giant covalent
Both are giant covalent structures because both have many atoms
Both consist of small molecules held by weak covalent bonds
Poly(ethene) is giant covalent; diamond has large molecules
mcqs.explain: The specification lists polymers as very large molecules and diamond as a giant covalent structure.

mcqs.q: A polymer is drawn as a repeating unit inside brackets with a subscript n. The n shows that:
options: the polymer molecule contains exactly n carbon atoms in total
the unit in the brackets is repeated a large number of times
the structure inside the brackets is a giant covalent lattice
n pairs of electrons are shared inside the repeating unit
mcqs.explain: The specification states that n is a large number, describing how many times the repeating unit occurs.

mcqs.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?
options: Two
One
Four
Three
mcqs.explain: Each oxygen atom (2,6) needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared, giving each atom eight outer electrons.

mcqs.q: In a dot and cross diagram of ammonia, NH3, the nitrogen atom is shown with:
options: three shared electrons and five that are not shared
three shared pairs and no other outer shell electrons
four shared pairs, with one spare pair to each hydrogen
three shared pairs and one pair that is not shared
mcqs.explain: Nitrogen is 2,5; three electrons are shared with hydrogen atoms and the remaining two form a non-bonding pair, giving eight outer electrons.

mcqs.q: In a displayed formula, what does one line drawn between two atoms represent?
options: One single electron passed from one atom to the other atom
The transfer of an electron from one atom to another atom
One shared pair of electrons, that is a single covalent bond
Two shared pairs of electrons held between the two atoms
mcqs.explain: The specification uses a line to represent a single bond, which is one shared pair of electrons.

mcqs.q: A ball and stick model shows one black ball joined by four sticks to four white balls. Black is carbon and white is hydrogen. The molecular formula is:
options: C4H4
CH
CH4
C4H
mcqs.explain: One carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms; the sticks are the four covalent bonds, not atoms.

mcqs.q: Why are the outer electrons in a metal able to move through the whole structure?
options: They are held loosely in the outer shell of their own atom
They are attracted to the negative ions within the lattice
They are shared in pairs between neighbouring metal atoms
They are delocalised, so they are not held by any one atom
mcqs.explain: The specification states that outer shell electrons are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.

mcqs.q: Which phrase describes the structure of a pure metal?
options: A giant structure of atoms joined by shared pairs of electrons
A giant structure of atoms arranged in a regular pattern
A lattice of positive and negative ions attracting each other
Small molecules of metal atoms packed closely together
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's description of the structure of a metal.
